title: Regional proxy handoff and traffic classification notes
content:
Purpose:
This note collects operational patterns and engineering tradeoffs for handing traffic between region-level proxies, classifying traffic into predictable classes, and ensuring mTLS/identity continuity during cross-region failover. Target audience: platform engineers, infra SREs, and product teams planning regional rollouts for Dedicated and Private deployments.

Background / motivation:
- We run customer workloads across multi-region clusters for locality, capacity, and DR.
- Edge routers (global) forward to regional ingress proxies; within a region we use a mesh (Envoy sidecars) for service-to-service.
- Problem: when we need to move a flow (or fail over) to another region, how do we hand off without breaking mTLS, audit logs, or session-affinity dependencies?

Goals:
- Minimize request disruption and preserve caller identity across region boundaries.
- Provide deterministic routing rules for different traffic classes (control vs. inference vs. admin).
- Keep complexity reasonable — minimal cross-region state sync.
- Make failure modes observable and safe (no silent request drops).

Constraints and assumptions:
- Customers may pin model versions to region-specific pools.
- Service mesh (Envoy) sidecars are default; we have a path for sidecarless proxies on host gateways.
- Inter-region latency varies (10–120ms); for latency-sensitive inference we prefer local handling.
- KMS keys are region-bound for Private deployments; cross-region calls may require re-encryption or key proxying.

Traffic classification (proposal):
- Traffic-Class A: Latency-sensitive inference (single-turn, <50ms target). Prefer local region, no automatic failover across regions unless explicitly configured by customer policy.
- Traffic-Class B: Throughput/elastic inference (background batch or async streaming). Allow cross-region load spreading and re-routing for capacity.
- Traffic-Class C: Control plane / admin calls (deploy, rollout, metrics ingestion). Should be routed to control-plane designated region(s) with strict auth and audit.

Policy primitives we will use:
- region_preference: prefer-local | prefer-closest | strict-local
- handoff_allowed: true|false
- handoff_strategy: immediate | drain-then-switch | mirrored-proxy
- identity_propagation: passthrough | re-issue | proxy-asserted

Proxy handoff patterns (detailed):
1) Passive failover (drain-then-switch) - safe default
  - Source region marks instance unhealthy, start draining.
  - Global ingress shifts new connections to target region.
  - Ingress includes X-Original-Region header and a handoff-token (signed) that target region can validate.
  - mTLS continuity: caller mTLS terminates at local regional edge. For handoff, we do NOT attempt to continue original TLS session; instead we rely on service identity propagation token to re-establish authenticated call in target region.
  - Pros: predictable, avoids in-flight decryption complexity. Cons: short window of reduced capacity, not seamless for long-lived streaming.

2) Active mirroring / shadow-proxy handoff - aggressive, for stateful flows
  - Global ingress duplicates traffic to both primary and candidate region for a short trial window.
  - Target region accepts but does not respond to client; after warm-up, ingress switches primary to target.
  - Requires parity of model versions and warmed caches.
  - mTLS continuity: same token-based identity issuance used; we avoid forwarding raw TLS.
  - Use case: migrations where cache/KV state must be pre-warmed.

3) L4 TCP-level pass-through with connection handoff (not recommended except for special cases)
  - Very hard to do across WAN. Needs consistent anycast or global L4 fabric.
  - Only consider for private deployments with SD-WAN.

Identity and mTLS considerations:
- We will not attempt to proxy raw TLS sessions across regions. Instead:
  - Caller mTLS terminates at regional edge and an identity token (JWT/mtls-signed assertion) is minted by the regional proxy.
  - Token contains: original-client-id, orig-region, timestamp, nonce, validity (short-lived), signature with regional control plane key.
  - Target region validates token against rotating trust bundle from control plane (cacheable).
  - For stricter policies we support re-issuing a fresh mTLS session within target region using the regional CA (proxy-asserted identity).

Control plane interactions and trust model:
- Central control plane (or tiered regional controllers) distributes trust bundles and handoff policies. Control plane writes: region-routing-policies, CA-bundles, signing-keys (private keys never leave KMS).
- Regions pull policies and trust metadata via authenticated SAS tokens (rotate every 24h).
- For Private on-prem installs, we provide local control plane mirrors; handoff tokens validate against local trust or via configured federated trust endpoint.

Service mesh (Envoy) specifics:
- Sidecar path: ingress -> regional gateway envoy -> local service envoy (sidecar). Handoff token presented at gateway and proxied to sidecar via x-forwarded-assertion header. Sidecar verifies assertion using in-cluster CA.
- Host gateway path (sidecarless): gateway attaches assertion and directly speaks to service over mTLS using node certificate (node-level identity).
- Circuit breakers: per-route circuit limits must be region-aware. When failing over, breaker state may not transfer; use conservative defaults to avoid cascading failures.

Caching and KV considerations:
- Sticky sessions tie to local cache (KV, model KV cache). When handing over, cold-cache miss risk exists. We mitigate by:
  - marking critical keys for pre-warm during mirror phase
  - using consistent-hash routing on keys where possible (prefer same region)
  - fallback to model-servable compressed checkpoint fetch with grace TTL if cache miss happens

Operational playbooks (short):
- Normal failover (regional outage):
  1) Global ingress marks region as degraded -> ingress shifts new requests to next preferred region (respecting traffic class).
  2) Ingress includes handoff-token header.
  3) Target region validates token, emits audit event.
  4) SRE monitors request error spike / user-impact, roll back if needed.
- Rollout (planned migration):
  1) Mirror warming: run mirrored traffic for 15–60m, check latency/p99 and cache hit rates.
  2) Promote target region with drain-then-switch.

Observability & telemetry:
- Handoff events: emit structured logs with fields: orig_region, target_region, token_id, traffic_class, model_version, reason.
- Traces should include handoff span with validated_flag. Tag traces where identity was re-issued.
- Alerts: high rate of handoffs for class A traffic, token validation failures > 0.1%/minute, mirrored warm-up error rate > 1%.

Security notes:
- Handoff tokens short-lived (30–120s) and single-use where possible. Token signing keys stored in KMS and never mirrored to regions in plaintext.
- Audit log of any proxy-assertion events must be immutable and exportable for compliance customers.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Q1: Should we support transparent TLS passthrough for enterprise SD-WAN customers? (If yes, scope and security requirements)
- Q2: Define consistent hashing key for model KV routing for embeddings and KV cache.
- Q3: Policy UX for customers to opt into cross-region failover per deployment (API + Console).
- TODO: implement token format RFC and small reference library for token mint/verify (Amina).
- TODO: define metrics dashboard for warm-up mirror phase (Diego).

Decision log (running):
- 2024-09-12: agreed default = drain-then-switch for Class A; allow mirrored warm-up for planned migrations.
- 2024-09-26: decided not to proxy raw TLS across regions; use signed handoff tokens instead.

Action items:
- Priya: write token RFC + example Envoy filter config for header injection. Due 2024-10-10.
- Diego: dashboard prototype for mirror warm-up metrics. Due 2024-10-03.
- Ethan: verify compatibility matrix for control-plane trust sync with Private deployments. Due 2024-10-17.

Appendix (example header payload):
  X-Handoff-Assertion: base64({"client_id":"acct:1234","orig_region":"us-west-2","token_id":"abc-987","exp":1697040000,"sig":"..."})

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep options small. Too many per-customer knobs -> operational nightmares.
- Default should be safest: no silent re-encryption or secret replication.
- Investigate sidecarless perf wins for high-throughput internal-only routes.

References:
- internal: confluence/geo-routing-strategy (linked above)
- envoy docs: TLS origination patterns
- prior tickets: PLAT-312 (cache pre-warm), PLAT-499 (mirror infra)

End of notes.
